idiom_name: duck typing with hasattr(), or @runtime_checkable Protocol + isinstance
implementation_notes: Python's query is duck typing with an explicit test: `hasattr(x, 'flush')` (or calling the operation and catching AttributeError) asks whether the object supports it, and since the typing module gained @runtime_checkable the same question can be declared - a Protocol decorated that way may be passed to isinstance, which performs a structural member check (PEP 544). What replaces the classic structure is this runtime structural check, with the same Protocol giving static type checkers the type at the same time. The typing documentation warns that the runtime form only checks that members exist, not their types, and can be 'surprisingly slow', which is why plain hasattr or the call-and-catch form is justified on hot paths and runtime_checkable protocols where the capability set is consumed as data (plugin registries).
pitfalls: runtime_checkable isinstance checks member presence only: a method with the wrong signature passes, and issubclass works only for non-data protocols.

hasattr can be wrong in both directions: an object with __getattr__ claims capabilities it cannot perform, while a property that raises AttributeError hides one it has - the call remains the real test.
Protocols used with isinstance must not be subscripted or generic, and data protocols are excluded from issubclass, so parameterised capabilities cannot be queried directly.
isinstance with protocols is markedly slower than a plain attribute check; reach for it for clarity, not in tight loops.
